Teaching a robot a new task takes weeks of expert work. And you repeat it for every new robot. What if one person, showing it once, was enough?

Robots are leaving the factory: arms, mobile manipulators, humanoids. Foundation models, like NVIDIA GR00T, are making them teachable by example. But the bottleneck remains: every new robot needs its own expert time. We built TransferGap to remove it.
Here is the catch. Copy a human demonstration onto a robot, and it works only about half the time. Thirty-one out of sixty on the UR5e. And nobody knows why.

TransferGap measures the person from a single video, copies the motion to each robot, and finds exactly which stage failed. Think of it as a doctor for robot learning: it finds the cause, not just the symptom. Then an NVIDIA Nemotron model, running through Nebius Token Factory, picks the fix, and we verify it in simulation.

Watch what happens. On the left, the plain copy of the human demonstration. On the right, the same robot after TransferGap's diagnosed fix. The UR5e goes from thirty-one to sixty out of sixty. The UR10e, from thirty-four to sixty. The KAIROS arm, from forty-eight to sixty. The same demonstration also drives a humanoid, a robot hand, and bigger objects. A seven centimeter cube goes from zero to fifty-six of sixty.

Then we go from copying to learning. One neural network, with no scripted controller, drives four different robots, and succeeds in all twelve test conditions. Two independent training runs, same result.
We used NVIDIA open models end to end: Nemotron on Nebius, a Cosmos critic that is ninety-six percent accurate, and a fine-tuned GR00T that reaches twenty-seven out of thirty.
One demonstration today. Every robot tomorrow.
TransferGap. From one person, to a fleet of robots.
